Systems Programming and Machine Organization
Chapter 26: Page Faults
Dr. Charles Dorner

1. A fault is a request for a decision, not always a disaster
Problem and first experiment

SAY
A page fault means the attempted memory access could not complete under the current translation or protection state. That can be part of normal demand paging, or it can reveal an invalid operation. The kernel must determine the address, requested access, and mapping policy before choosing recovery. A valid anonymous page may receive zero-filled backing; a forbidden write may be rejected. It is therefore misleading to say every page fault means a crash or every page fault means a disk read. Our programs safely model these policy choices without deliberately dereferencing invalid memory or trying to recover from corrupted application state.

DO
Ask for the concrete state change or units before revealing the explanation.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch26.json → SP26.010: 26.4 Fault handling

------------------------------------------------------------

2. Classify before allocating
Problem and first experiment

SAY
The program asks four policy questions without accessing any page. An absent anonymous region yields demand-zero. A write to a read-only region yields deny. A write to a copy-on-write region yields private-write, while a read of a present read-only region can resume. The printed words are decisions in a simplified function, not proof that a kernel allocated memory or raised an exception. The order matters: an invalid region must not be granted storage merely because it lacks a present page. A real handler has more states and synchronization duties, but it preserves the same distinction between logical permission and current backing.

DO
Predict every line, run the complete example, then state exactly which behavior the result establishes.

Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch26.json → SP26.004: 26.1 Missing pages

------------------------------------------------------------

3. Demand-zero need not involve a storage device
Problem and first experiment

SAY
A program can reserve anonymous memory without touching every page. When it first accesses a legitimate page, the kernel can supply zero-initialized backing according to the mapping contract. No existing file contents need to be read for that demand-zero case. A file-backed fault is different, and even then the required data may already be in the operating system’s cache. Counting all faults together therefore mixes operations with very different costs. When a workload gets slower, distinguish fault type, amount of backing work, and storage waiting before blaming the device. The same number of page faults can correspond to very different elapsed time.

DO
Ask for the concrete state change or units before revealing the explanation.

content/systems-programming/ch26.json → SP26.016: Worked example — Demand-zero allocation

------------------------------------------------------------

4. Private writing copies only the model page that needs separation
Problem and first experiment

SAY
Our page objects contain two integers each. Parent and child initially share both objects. The first child write to page zero sees another owner and creates a private copy. A second write to that same page changes the exclusive copy without another allocation, leaving the copy counter at one. The final output is parent seven, child eleven, copies one; the untouched second page remains shared. This is an ownership model in one C++ process, not an actual fork or hardware page fault. It illustrates the private-modification guarantee and why one should not promise that every later write requires a new physical copy.

DO
Predict every line, run the complete example, then state exactly which behavior the result establishes.

6. Where the simple approach fails
The chapter problem

SAY
This single-threaded smart-pointer model is not an OS page-fault handler. Checking unique() is not a safe general concurrent copy-on-write protocol.

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Write through child before making the private copy. The parent observes the mutation before separation occurs.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Prepare private backing first, then write it. Keep the thread-safety and lifetime assumptions explicit.

7. Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
The chapter problem

SAY
Copying the old value before assignment preserves the private-write contract. If allocation throws, the assignment to owner has not yet committed and the original shared value remains intact. unique() is suitable only under this lab’s single-threaded access rule; it does not establish a safe concurrent mutation protocol. OS copy-on-write applies similar intent at a different boundary.

A plausible alternative: Eager copying is simpler when data is small or almost every element will change.

8. Chapter 26 — Page Faults
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A page fault is an architectural notification that a memory access could not proceed under the current translation and protection state. The kernel interprets the event in the context of the process’s mappings. Some faults are routine mechanisms for implementing valid memory behavior; others reveal an invalid access. [ R3 , R10 , R14 ]

10. Missing pages
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A missing translation can correspond to a legitimate region whose physical backing has not yet been installed. Anonymous memory can be provided lazily, and file-backed mappings can bring in pages as needed. Deferring work avoids allocating and reading pages that the application never touches. A missing page can also correspond to no valid mapping at all. The handler must consult the mapping policy rather than assume that any requested address deserves storage. Otherwise, invalid pointers would silently create new memory instead of being rejected.

In plain English: The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

DO

11. Protection faults
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A protection fault occurs when a mapping exists or is described, but the attempted operation is not permitted by the active protection state. Writing to a read-only mapping and fetching instructions from a non-executable mapping are examples under the relevant hardware configuration. Some protection faults are intentionally recoverable, notably copy-on-write. Others indicate an error. The handler must distinguish the region’s logical policy from its current hardware permission bits. A read-only code page is not made writable simply because a process attempted a store.

DO

12. Demand paging
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Demand paging supplies a page when it is actually needed. For a file mapping, the kernel can obtain the corresponding file data; for anonymous memory, it can provide zero-initialized storage consistent with the mapping’s semantics. Existing cached data can avoid a new storage-device read. The performance consequence depends on the work required. Some faults can be satisfied without reading from storage; others wait for I/O. A fault count without classification and workload context is therefore an incomplete performance metric. The same number of faults can represent very different elapsed costs.

DO

13. Fault handling
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Conceptually, handling involves identifying the faulting address and access, locating the mapping policy, validating the operation, obtaining suitable backing, updating translation structures, and resuming or rejecting the instruction. The kernel must synchronize this work with concurrent mapping changes and other faults. Application error handling usually does not attempt to repair arbitrary invalid pointer faults. Recovering from a corrupted execution state is much harder than catching a normal return-code error. Design programs to prevent invalid access and use operating-system errors for expected resource failures. Signal handling is discussed separately in Chapter 41.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.

14. Copy-on-write
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Copy-on-write lets logically independent mappings share backing until a writer requires a private version. After fork , parent and child can initially share many physical pages while observing private-memory semantics. A write fault can cause the kernel to create a private copy for the writer and update its mapping. [ R15 ] A physical copy is not mandatory in every write-fault case. If the kernel determines that the backing is no longer shared in a way requiring separation, it may be able to make the page writable without copying. The semantic guarantee is private modification, not a promise that every store invokes a particular copying algorithm.

15. A model of private modification
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
The following model uses immutable Python bytes as initial shared content and returns a new object when a private writer changes a byte. It demonstrates the observable contract of copy-on-write; it does not claim to implement page tables or reproduce the kernel’s physical allocation decisions. Companion listing: ch26/cow_model.py The expected output is ABCD AXCD . The model copies the entire small object for every store, which is deliberately simpler than a page-based implementation. Its value is that the ownership and visibility contract can be checked without relying on process scheduling or privileged inspection. The model also clarifies a boundary: a shared mapping would require a different contract. Making a private copy is correct for private modification but wrong for a communication region whose purpose is to expose one participant’s writes to another.

16. Demand-zero allocation
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A process may reserve a new virtual page without immediately receiving a physical frame. The first write faults because no frame is present. The kernel allocates a zeroed frame, installs a writable mapping, and restarts the instruction. The application experiences ordinary memory semantics while physical allocation is deferred until use.

17. Copy-on-write after fork
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
After fork , parent and child can initially map the same physical page read-only. If the child writes it, a protection fault lets the kernel allocate a private copy, copy the original contents, and remap the child’s page writable. The parent’s mapping still references the original frame. Copying is paid only for pages actually modified.

21. Copy-on-write separates logical permission from the current hardware bit
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A copy-on-write region may be logically allowed to change even though its current hardware mapping denies a direct store. That temporary protection lets the kernel intervene when a private version becomes necessary. A permanently read-only code mapping can use a similar-looking protection bit but has a different policy: a write is an error. The handler therefore needs more than the leaf writable bit to decide what recovery is allowed. Our classification program uses an explicit region kind to make that missing policy visible. Real kernels maintain richer metadata and coordinate it with mappings and other threads.

DO
Ask for the concrete state change or units before revealing the explanation.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch26.json → SP26.006: 26.2 Protection faults

------------------------------------------------------------

22. Resume only after the required invariant is restored
Reason about the implementation

SAY
The conceptual recovery path checks policy, obtains suitable backing, updates translation information, and then allows the operation to resume when permitted. Each step establishes a condition needed by the next. Resuming too early would repeat the unresolved access or expose wrong storage. Rejecting an invalid access is not a failure of demand paging; it is enforcement of the boundary. Real implementations also handle concurrent mapping changes and several threads faulting on related storage. Our models intentionally omit those races. A function that returns a policy word does not claim to perform page-table updates, translation invalidation, or instruction restart.

DO
Ask for the concrete state change or units before revealing the explanation.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch26.json → SP26.010: 26.4 Fault handling

------------------------------------------------------------

23. The shared_ptr demonstration has its own lifetime contract
Reason about the implementation

SAY
In the source lab, private_write receives a shared_ptr by reference so it can replace the caller’s owner when detaching. A by-value parameter would replace only the local handle and leave the caller referring to the earlier object. The function rejects a null owner before examining or dereferencing it. These are C++ ownership rules within the teaching model. Shared_ptr’s ownership bookkeeping does not make simultaneous writes to the pointed-to integer safe, and testing uniqueness is not a full concurrent copy-on-write protocol. The examples are single-threaded and bounded. If concurrent access becomes a requirement, design synchronization and publication separately rather than assuming the smart pointer supplies them.

DO
Ask for the concrete state change or units before revealing the explanation.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch26.json → SYS26.03: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits

------------------------------------------------------------

24. A source model is not a measurement of kernel copying
Reason about the implementation

SAY
Our model increments copies when make_shared creates another page object. That is an exact observation about this C++ program. It is not a count of physical pages copied by the operating system. After a real fork, the kernel may determine that a backing page no longer needs separation and simply change permissions instead. It may also use mechanisms whose granularity differs from our tiny model pages. The stable concept is that a private writer must not alter another logically independent view. Keep semantic tests and implementation measurements separate so a correct optimization is not mistaken for violating an overly specific classroom story.

DO
Ask for the concrete state change or units before revealing the explanation.

29. Copy on write separates values only when needed
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
Copy on write separates values only when needed. If another owner shares the integer, allocate a new integer initialized from the old one and make child own it. This single-threaded decision is not a concurrent ownership protocol.

Two private address-space models initially share a value of 7. A write in the child should leave the parent’s value unchanged.

Sharing unchanged storage saves a copy. The model checks sharing before allowing mutation. The copy preserves the promise that private modifications are independent.

If another owner shares the integer, allocate a new integer initialized from the old one and make child own it. This single-threaded decision is not a concurrent ownership protocol.

Dereferencing child now reaches the private integer, so writing 9 leaves parent’s integer unchanged.

The two reads print 7 and 9. Copy-on-write delays separation until a writer needs independent state.

A private writer detaches shared backing before changing the value. This ownership-count check is used only in the stated single-threaded model.

This single-threaded smart-pointer model is not an OS page-fault handler. Checking unique() is not a safe general concurrent copy-on-write protocol. In the extended lab: Write through child before making the private copy. The parent observes the mutation before separation occurs.

40. Chapter summary and maintenance
Recall and transfer

SAY
Copying the old value before assignment preserves the private-write contract. If allocation throws, the assignment to owner has not yet committed and the original shared value remains intact. unique() is suitable only under this lab’s single-threaded access rule; it does not establish a safe concurrent mutation protocol. OS copy-on-write applies similar intent at a different boundary.

Choose a simpler approach when its narrower contract is enough. Eager copying is simpler when data is small or almost every element will change.

When this system changes, retain a check that exposes the known failure: Write through child before making the private copy. The parent observes the mutation before separation occurs. Prepare private backing first, then write it. Keep the thread-safety and lifetime assumptions explicit.

41. Do not use arbitrary invalid accesses as normal error handling
Recall and transfer

SAY
A parser expecting malformed input should validate its lengths and return an error rather than deliberately writing beyond a buffer and hoping a signal handler can recover. A protection fault can happen after other mutations already occurred, and corrupted state may no longer support ordinary execution safely. The chapter therefore separates normal system-call error handling from attempts to repair arbitrary invalid pointer use. Our fault models use enum values and policy functions so they can be exercised safely and deterministically. When testing production code, use appropriate memory diagnostics and targeted bounds checks rather than treating a crash as the required validation path.

DO
Ask for the concrete state change or units before revealing the explanation.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch26.json → SP26.010: 26.4 Fault handling

------------------------------------------------------------

42. Review the observation before explaining the cost
Recall and transfer

SAY
To explain a page-fault report, start with what the counter actually means. Identify whether the mapping was legitimate, whether the access was a read or write, and whether recovery needed zero-fill, private separation, cached file data, or storage I/O. Then ask how that work sits on the application’s critical path. A single fault count cannot answer all these questions. The source model provides a small ownership lesson; our added examples provide policy and page-granularity lessons. Together they support debugging without pretending to implement a kernel. Extend tests by checking repeated private writes and untouched shared pages, then measure actual platform behavior separately.

DO
Ask for the concrete state change or units before revealing the explanation.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch26.json → SP26.020: Guided lab and review
